name: Untap UK claims rules: Delay Repay, UK261 and EU261, TfL refunds and dispute schemes
description: Every rule Untap applies to UK train delay, flight delay and Transport for London refund claims, one record per rule: Delay Repay thresholds, payout tiers and claim forms for each train operator, where to claim from each airline and its dispute scheme, TfL refund windows and thresholds, and the UK261 and EU261 compensation bands, ombudsmen and time limits. Each record names its sources, the date each was last checked and a version that changes when the rule does.
citation: Untap (2026). Untap UK claims rules: Delay Repay, UK261 and EU261, TfL refunds and dispute schemes. Version 2026-10-05.65c95941. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. https://untap.money/open-data/rules
notes: last_checked is the oldest date among a record’s sources. verification is the weakest way a load-bearing source was read: statute, live, archive, untap_guide, search_snippet, unverified or untap_practice.
version changes only when a rule’s values, claim URL or sources change. Re-checking a source does not change it.
These are the rules Untap applies. Before relying on one, check it with the company or regulator named in its sources.

records.subject: Avanti West Coast
records.summary: Pays from 15 minutes late: 25% of the single fare from 15 minutes, 50% from 30, 100% from 60. On a return ticket, one direction 120 minutes or more late pays the whole return fare. A cancelled journey is refunded at 100% of the single fare. Claim within 28 days on the operator’s own form.

values.automatic_scope: Advance tickets bought directly from Avanti, opt-in
values.rules_note: Table row: 120 or more, 100% on single, return and season
values.escalation: Rail Ombudsman

records.subject: Incomplete journeys
records.summary: Wait 48 hours before claiming, because TfL corrects many incomplete journeys automatically.

records.summary: Using two different cards or devices for one journey is treated as an incomplete journey, with the same 8-week window and the same form.

sources.name: Transport for London

records.subject: Hopper fare
records.summary: Bus and tram journeys started within 60 minutes of the tap that opens the Hopper window are free after the first fare. A charged tap inside that window is a missed Hopper fare.

sources.name: Transport for London

records.subject: Hopper fare
records.summary: Untap treats a missed Hopper fare as claimable for the same 8 weeks as an incomplete journey.

records.subject: UK261 short band
records.summary: £220 per passenger for a flight up to 1,500 km arriving 3 hours or more late, or cancelled. Half (£110) only where a cancelled flight’s replacement arrived less than 2 hours late.

sources.name: Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 retained in UK law, Article 7

records.subject: UK261 medium band
records.summary: £350 per passenger for a flight 1,500 to 3,500 km arriving 3 hours or more late, or cancelled. Half (£175) only where a cancelled flight’s replacement arrived less than 3 hours late.

sources.name: Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 retained in UK law, Article 7

records.subject: UK261 long band
records.summary: £520 per passenger for a flight over 3,500 km arriving 3 hours or more late, or cancelled. Half (£260) for an arrival delay of 3 to 4 hours.

sources.name: Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 retained in UK law, Article 7

records.subject: EU261 short band
records.summary: €250 per passenger for a flight up to 1,500 km arriving 3 hours or more late, or cancelled. Half (€125) only where a cancelled flight’s replacement arrived less than 2 hours late.

sources.name: Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 as adopted by the EU, Article 7

records.subject: EU261 medium band
records.summary: €400 per passenger for a flight 1,500 to 3,500 km arriving 3 hours or more late, or cancelled. Half (€200) only where a cancelled flight’s replacement arrived less than 3 hours late. A flight between two EU airports of more than 1,500 km is paid at this band, however long it is.

sources.name: Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 as adopted by the EU, Article 7

records.subject: EU261 long band
records.summary: €600 per passenger for a flight over 3,500 km arriving 3 hours or more late, or cancelled. Half (€300) for an arrival delay of 3 to 4 hours. Not for a flight between two EU airports, which stays at the medium band.

sources.name: Regulation (EC) No 261/2004 as adopted by the EU, Article 7

records.subject: Rail Ombudsman
records.summary: Once 40 working days have passed since complaining to the operator, or sooner on a final response (a deadlock letter, email or text) the person is unhappy with. Delay and cancellation disputes are in scope; it is free, and its decision binds the operator if the person accepts it. Within 12 months of the operator’s final response, unless circumstances are exceptional.

values.when: Once 40 working days have passed since complaining to the operator, or sooner on a final response (a deadlock letter, email or text) the person is unhappy with. Delay and cancellation disputes are in scope; it is free, and its decision binds the operator if the person accepts it.
values.time_limit: Within 12 months of the operator’s final response, unless circumstances are exceptional.

sources.name: Rail Ombudsman: frequently asked questions

records.subject: Rail delay claim handling
records.summary: Under the rail regulator’s Delay Compensation Code of Practice, operators process a correctly completed claim within 20 working days, tell the passenger within 5 working days if evidence is missing, and give written reasons and a way to contest a refusal.

sources.name: ORR Delay Compensation Code of Practice, paragraphs 4.1 to 4.6

records.subject: Rail claim deadline
records.summary: Compensation is claimed from the train company responsible for the delay. A claim sent to any train company whose trains were used is passed on to the right one. Claims go in within 28 days of finishing the journey.

sources.name: National Rail Conditions of Travel (from 30 July 2026), Conditions 32 and 33

records.subject: Airline final response
records.summary: If the airline refuses, or has not given a final answer within 8 weeks of the written claim, the case can go to the airline’s dispute scheme or, if it has none, to the CAA.

sources.name: Civil Aviation Authority: alternative dispute resolution

records.subject: AviationADR
records.summary: After a written complaint to the airline through its own procedure, and either its final written response (deadlock letter) or 8 weeks without one. Free for passengers; the decision binds the airline once the passenger accepts it. Within 12 months of the airline’s final response, or of the last contact if it never replied.

values.when: After a written complaint to the airline through its own procedure, and either its final written response (deadlock letter) or 8 weeks without one. Free for passengers; the decision binds the airline once the passenger accepts it.
values.time_limit: Within 12 months of the airline’s final response, or of the last contact if it never replied.

sources.name: AviationADR: what to do before you apply

records.subject: CEDR aviation adjudication
records.summary: Once 8 weeks have passed since the first complaint without a settlement, or the airline says it cannot resolve it, or it could not be reached despite reasonable efforts. Free for passengers; the decision binds the airline once the passenger accepts it. Within 12 months of the deadlock notice, or of the last attempt to contact the airline if there was none.

values.when: Once 8 weeks have passed since the first complaint without a settlement, or the airline says it cannot resolve it, or it could not be reached despite reasonable efforts. Free for passengers; the decision binds the airline once the passenger accepts it.
values.time_limit: Within 12 months of the deadlock notice, or of the last attempt to contact the airline if there was none.

sources.name: CEDR Aviation Adjudication Scheme Rules, March 2026

records.subject: Civil Aviation Authority complaints team (PACT)
records.summary: For a UK261 claim on an airline in no approved dispute scheme, after a written complaint and an unsatisfactory answer or 8 weeks without one. PACT gives a view and raises it with the airline but cannot impose a decision. PACT does not take a complaint with less than a year left to go to court.

values.when: For a UK261 claim on an airline in no approved dispute scheme, after a written complaint and an unsatisfactory answer or 8 weeks without one. PACT gives a view and raises it with the airline but cannot impose a decision.
values.time_limit: PACT does not take a complaint with less than a year left to go to court.

sources.name: Civil Aviation Authority: how the CAA can help (PACT)

records.subject: UK261 court time limit
records.summary: A UK261 claim can be taken to court within six years of the flight in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and five years in Scotland.

sources.name: Civil Aviation Authority: how the CAA can help (PACT)

records.subject: EU261 court time limit
records.summary: EU261 sets no time limit of its own: the period is set by the national law of the country where the claim is brought (Cuadrench Moré v KLM, C-139/11). Untap does not hold a table of those periods, so no date is given. A dispute scheme can have its own time limit.

sources.name: Cuadrench Moré v KLM, Case C-139/11 (CJEU, 22 November 2012)

records.subject: London TravelWatch
records.summary: After complaining to TfL and asking for a manager’s review, if the outcome or the handling is still not right. It expects TfL to have had 20 working days to reply and cannot force TfL to agree. London Overground and Elizabeth line complaints go to the Rail Ombudsman instead. No fixed limit, but complaints have to be raised within a reasonable time; London TravelWatch notes most come within six weeks of the problem.
